sections.history: Maanthurai lies a few kilometres before Lalgudi on the road from Tiruchirappalli, in the fertile country north of the Kaveri. In the Tevaram hymns it is Tirumaandurai, one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams of Chola Nadu, sung by the saint Sambandar and, according to tradition, by Appar as well. The name is read as the landing place of the mango: maa is the mango tree and thurai a bank or ford, and the shrine is remembered as standing in an ancient mango forest, which is why the Lord is called Amravaneswarar, Lord of the Mango Grove. The early shrine was raised in stone and greatly enlarged by Chola rulers, with the major expansion placed in the eleventh century, and worship has continued without a break since.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a three-tiered rajagopuram, and at the main entrance stand sculpted figures of Ganesha and Murugan, one on either side. Passing in, the visitor enters the main prakara, where the sanctum of Amravaneswarar holds the Shiva linga, and the goddess Azhagammai, also called Balambikai, is honoured in her own shrine within the enclosure. A temple tank lies close at hand. Stucco work within the complex gives the legend of the deer worshipping beneath the mango tree a visible form, so that the story the village is named for can be read on the walls.
sections.legends: The story of Maanthurai is the story of the deer and the mango. A sage, cursed to be born as a deer, is said to have come to this grove and worshipped Shiva beneath a mango tree. Pleased by his devotion, the Lord freed him from the curse and bestowed a mango upon the deer, and the place has been called Maanthurai ever since. The freed sage then asked that Shiva and Parvati remain here for ever, and so they dwell in the temple as Amravaneswarar and Balambikai. A second tradition recalls the sage Mrigandu, who worshipped the Lord here to be granted a son, the boy Markandeya who overcame death, and the village is sometimes spoken of as his birthplace.
sections.festivals: The great festival is the Chithirai festival, kept over fifteen days in the Tamil month of Chithirai, April to May, in which the incidents of the temple's legend are brought to life. The temple keeps six daily rituals and some twelve festivals through the year. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Maanthurai suits a slow and quiet visit. Enter beneath the eastern gopuram, greet Ganesha and Murugan at the door, and walk the prakara to the sanctum of Amravaneswarar before turning to the gentle goddess Azhagammai in her own shrine. Look for the stucco figures that tell of the deer and the mango, and sit for a while near the tank. Few pilgrims come here compared with the great temples of nearby Tiruchirappalli, and that is much of its charm: within the walls, the village keeps the stillness of the old mango grove.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 7:00 to 11:30 in the morning and from about 4:30 to 7:30 in the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is appreciated: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is usually permitted in the outer courtyards but not inside the sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple practice. Please ask the temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Maanthurai is about 15 km from Tiruchirappalli on the Tiruchirappalli–Lalgudi road, roughly 3 km before Lalgudi, and town buses run along that road. Tiruchirappalli is the main railway junction and has the nearest airport. The temple stands in the village, a short walk or auto ride from the bus stop on the main road.
